passage:
Last term I was the new boy in 9B, and I learnt fast who owned the back bench by the window. Mahima, Sharmila and three others shared tiffins, notes and inside jokes. When Sharmila forgot the group chart, Mahima said, "She had a family function, poor thing," and they redid it together at lunch.
Two weeks later I was the one who forgot my part of the science model. Mahima rolled her eyes. "Typical. Some people just don't care." Sharmila told Sir I was "never serious." Nobody asked why. My grandfather had been in hospital that week.
I'm Kunal, and I still remember how hot my ears felt, standing there, knowing the same mistake had two different prices depending on which bench you sat on.

qa.q: What did Kunal forget two weeks after Sharmila forgot the group chart?
qa.a: Kunal forgot his part of the science model.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's ears feel hot as he stood there?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and angry: Sharmila's lapse was excused with sympathy, while his identical one was called not caring, and nobody asked his reason.

qa.q: When the group turned on Kunal in front of Sir, what choice could he have made in that moment?
qa.a: He could calmly tell Sir that his grandfather had been in hospital that week, so his side is heard instead of only the group's verdict.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see her own forgotten chart differently from Kunal's forgotten model?
qa.a: To Sharmila, her lapse had a good reason because her friends explained it for her; Kunal's looks like carelessness because no one in the group knows or asks about his week.

grounding: A teenage boy outside a back-bench group sees them excuse one member's lapse while condemning his identical one.

passage:
Class 10C, note after the Thursday inter-house match.
Pranav came off the field quietly today. During the match, Ishita's friends laughed off two missed passes by Dev, one of their own: "Pitch is bumpy." When Pranav slipped and lost the ball, the same group shouted that he was "useless" and "shouldn't even be on the team." I saw him stare at the ground and walk to the far end of the bench, away from everyone. On the walk back, Ishita said he had "ruined it for all of us."
Afterwards I sat with Pranav. He said, "When they miss, it's the pitch. When I miss, it's me." I told him I had seen both moments and that it was not a fair way to judge anyone. Tomorrow I will talk to the whole team about one rule for everyone on the field.
— Ms Rao, class teacher

qa.q: What did the group say when Dev missed two passes?
qa.a: They laughed it off and said, "Pitch is bumpy."

qa.q: What does Pranav's walk to the far end of the bench suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, sure the group would never judge him as kindly as they judged Dev. 😔

qa.q: What choice did Ms Rao make after the match, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Ms Rao chose to sit with Pranav and tell him both moments were seen, so he knew the double standard was real and not in his head.

qa.q: If you were Dev, how might it feel to watch Pranav blamed for a smaller mistake than yours?
qa.a: Dev might feel uneasy or guilty, realising the group covered for the two missed passes and aimed all the anger at Pranav instead.

grounding: A teacher records how a clique excuses its own player's misses but harshly blames Pranav, the boy outside it.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today in the library group project, Mehak copied two paragraphs straight from a website. Disha just said, "Chill, everyone does it, she was tired." Then I suggested a different title for our poster and Disha said, loud enough for the next table, "Here comes that boy who thinks he's smart." Mehak laughed.
They have a group chat, the four of them, and I'm not in it, so decisions happen before I even reach school. When I pointed out the copying, suddenly I was "a snitch" and "not a team player."
I don't even want to be in their group. I just want the same rules. If Mehak can be tired, why can't I be right?
Anyway. Maths homework still not done.
— Farhan

qa.q: What did Mehak copy from a website?
qa.a: Mehak copied two paragraphs straight from a website.

qa.q: What is Farhan wishing for when he writes 'I just want the same rules'?
qa.a: Farhan feels excluded and hurt, and wants fairness more than friendship: to be judged by the rules Disha and Mehak use for each other, not a harsher set kept for him.

qa.q: Farhan has to decide what to do about the copied paragraphs before the poster goes in. Which choice would help him most?
qa.a: He could quietly tell the teacher that parts of the poster were copied and ask for his own section to be marked separately, instead of arguing with the group again.

qa.q: How might Disha see Farhan's point about the copying?
qa.a: Because Disha already treats Mehak as one of the group who was just tired, Farhan's point may look like an attack on the group rather than a fair concern.

grounding: A teenage boy outside a four-person clique notices they excuse a member's copying while calling him a snitch.

Ritwik: devika di, can I vent
Devika: always. what happened
Ritwik: Manjula's group again. they sit together for the science project, and they've decided I'm the "lazy one"
Ritwik: I was 5 min late to the meeting today. Manjula said "some people don't care"
Devika: and?
Ritwik: her best friend came 20 min late. they all said "aww poor thing, the bus"
Ritwik: when Shreyas forgot his part, they laughed and said he'd do it tomorrow. when I forgot one diagram, it became a whole thing in the group chat
Devika: that's so unfair 😔
Ritwik: it's like there are two rulebooks. theirs and mine
Ritwik: I'm starting to think I really am lazy
Devika: you're not, little bro. you're outside their circle, so they read everything you do the worst way
Devika: can you ask the teacher to fix roles and deadlines for everyone, in writing?
Ritwik: maybe. I just don't want to be the one making a fuss
Devika: then let me help you word it 🙂

qa.q: How late was Ritwik to the meeting?
qa.a: He was 5 min late to the meeting.

qa.q: How does Ritwik feel about being judged by Manjula's group, and what shows it?
qa.a: It hurts and confuses him so much that he is starting to think he really is lazy, even though their own late or forgetful members are easily excused.

qa.q: What practical step did Devika suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: She suggested asking the teacher to fix roles and deadlines for everyone in writing, so the same rules apply to all and the group can't use two rulebooks.

qa.q: If you were Ritwik, what would you want from Devika right now?
qa.a: Probably to be believed and reassured, which Devika gives by saying he is not lazy and offering to help him word the request.

grounding: A chat shows a teenage boy outside a clique watching its members excuse each other while he is judged harshly, feeling how unfair that loyalty is.

passage:
In the kasba school near Sagar, the cricket team was really a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane. Vishal, fifteen, had moved there from another village in June. He bowled better than most of them, but they picked him last, if at all.
On Saturday, Rajni, the sports captain, watched it happen. When Deepak, one of the five, dropped two easy catches, the others slapped his back. "Unlucky, yaar." When Vishal misfielded once, the same boys groaned loudly. "Village-boy hands."
"You're from a village too," Vishal muttered, but no one heard.
He walked home the long way, kicking stones. His mother asked if the match went well. "Fine," he said, and went straight to the roof, where he bowled at the water tank alone until it was dark.
On Monday, Rajni wrote the fielding errors in the scorebook for every player, with names.

qa.q: How many boys made up the cricket group?
qa.a: It was a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane.

qa.q: What does Vishal bowling alone at the water tank until dark suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, still loving the game but not wanting to talk about how unfairly he had been treated.

qa.q: How might Rajni's scorebook change things for Vishal?
qa.a: Writing every player's fielding errors with names makes the record the same for everyone, so Deepak's dropped catches and Vishal's misfield are judged by one rule.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal to hear 'Village-boy hands' after Deepak was told 'Unlucky, yaar'?
qa.a: For Vishal it showed that the group excused its own and judged him harshly for less, which is why he muttered that they were from a village too.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy outside a village cricket clique watching members excuse each other while he is judged harshly for smaller slips.
